exercise1.prompt: transform versus aggregate: Rows above their own group

hiddenCases.name: a group of one is never above its own mean
the comparison is against the group, not the table

exercise1.hint: transform("mean") gives each row its group average, which lines up with the table so you can compare row by row. An aggregate would collapse the groups and leave you nothing to compare against.

exercise2.prompt: transform versus aggregate: Each row as a share of its group

hiddenCases.name: a row alone in its group is all of it
the total is the group’s, not the table’s

exercise2.hint: transform("sum") gives each row its group total, lined up with the table. Divide, multiply by 100, round, and tolist().

questions.prompt: How does transform differ from agg?
choices: transform returns one value per row; agg returns one per group
questions.explain: Which is what makes transform the way to put a group mean beside every row.

questions.prompt: You want each row compared with its own group’s mean. What do you use?
questions.explain: An aggregate throws away the rows, leaving nothing to compare against.

questions.prompt: A 4-row table with 2 groups. How long is the transform result?
questions.explain: Same length and same index as the table, which is what lets it become a column.

questions.prompt: Why is "above own group mean" different from "above table mean"?
choices: A group with high values has a high bar of its own
questions.explain: A row can beat the table and not beat its own group, and reporting one as the other is a different claim.
